## Terraform infrastructure management guide

*Generated by: GPT-5.6-Sol (medium)*

Terraform treats every .tf file in one directory as a single configuration. The filenames are for human organization; Terraform determines creation order from references between resources.

We currently have two independent Terraform configurations:

- infra/bootstrap: already applied; manages Terraform state storage and GitHub’s AWS identities.
- infra/platform: implemented and tested, but not applied; defines the application environment.

A few basic Terraform terms:

- terraform: configures Terraform itself and its providers/backend.
- provider: configures the AWS connection and safety limits.
- variable: an input supplied by us.
- locals: calculated values used internally.
- data: reads something that already exists in AWS.
- resource: something Terraform creates or manages.
- output: a value Terraform reports after planning or applying.

## Bootstrap configuration

The bootstrap stack solves a chicken-and-egg problem: Terraform needs remote storage for its state, but that storage first has to be created.

versions.tf (infra/bootstrap/versions.tf)

- Requires Terraform 1.17.x.
- Declares the HashiCorp AWS provider and its permitted version range.
- The adjacent lockfile pins the exact provider version actually selected.

backend.tf (infra/bootstrap/backend.tf)

- Declares that this stack’s state is stored in an S3 backend.
- The bucket, state-object key, region, profile, and locking settings come from the ignored backend.tfbackend file.
- The bootstrap initially used local state, created the bucket, and was then migrated into that bucket under bootstrap/terraform.tfstate.

variables.tf (infra/bootstrap/variables.tf)

Defines configurable inputs and validates them:

- Expected AWS account ID.
- AWS region and local CLI profile.
- GitHub owner and repository.
- Protected GitHub environment names.
- Whether Terraform should create or reuse GitHub’s account-level OIDC provider.

The account and region validations help prevent accidentally modifying the wrong AWS environment.

main.tf (infra/bootstrap/main.tf)

Creates the bootstrap resources:

- Configures the AWS provider with an account allowlist and common tags.
- Creates the S3 bucket used for Terraform state.
- Enables S3 versioning and server-side encryption.
- Blocks all public access.
- Adds a policy rejecting non-TLS access.
- Creates or reuses GitHub’s OIDC identity provider.
- Creates separate GitHub roles for infrastructure plans and applies.
- Restricts those roles to this repository and the protected GitHub environments.
- Attaches the state-access policies defined in policies.tf.

The plan and apply roles are separate because planning usually needs less authority than changing infrastructure.

policies.tf (infra/bootstrap/policies.tf)

Builds the IAM policy documents for the two GitHub roles:

- The plan role can read the platform state and manage only its lock file.
- The apply role can read and update the platform state and its lock file.
- Both are restricted to learning/platform.tfstate, not the entire bucket.

These policies currently grant state-storage access only. AWS permissions for managing the application infrastructure belong to the next delivery-operations unit.

outputs.tf (infra/bootstrap/outputs.tf)

Reports values needed by later work:

- GitHub plan-role ARN.
- GitHub apply-role ARN.
- GitHub OIDC-provider ARN.
- Terraform state-bucket name.
- Reserved platform-state key.

Outputs are references to created infrastructure—not secrets.

## Application-platform configuration

This stack uses the bootstrap bucket for its own independent state at learning/platform.tfstate.

versions.tf (infra/platform/versions.tf)

- Requires Terraform 1.17.x.
- Declares the AWS provider.
- The lockfile currently selects AWS provider 6.73.0.

backend.tf (infra/platform/backend.tf)

- Declares the same S3 remote-state mechanism.
- Its backend configuration points to learning/platform.tfstate.
- Native S3 locking prevents two Terraform operations from updating this state simultaneously.

variables.tf (infra/platform/variables.tf)

Defines the stack’s external inputs:

- Expected AWS account and region.
- Whether to authenticate through the local AWS profile or ambient GitHub OIDC credentials.
- Two supported Availability Zone IDs.
- Exact immutable container-image digest.
- OpenAI model identifier.
- ECS desired task count.

Important constraints include:

- Only us-east-1 is accepted.
- CloudFront’s unsupported use1-az3 is rejected.
- The container image must be identified by a valid SHA-256 digest.
- The service may run zero or one task only.
- Zero tasks is the default, preventing an accidental deployment before its image and secret are ready.

main.tf (infra/platform/main.tf)

Contains shared configuration and calculated values:

- Configures the AWS provider and expected account.
- Supports either the local Identity Center profile or GitHub OIDC credentials.
- Applies common project/environment tags.
- Defines consistent resource names.
- Constructs the exact ECR image reference from the repository URL and digest.
- Calculates CloudFront and Cognito callback URLs.
- Defines the operators authorization group.
- Defines the six subnet CIDR ranges and their roles.

These locals avoid repeating important names and addresses across files.

network.tf (infra/platform/network.tf)

Defines the network foundation:

- One VPC with DNS enabled.
- One internet gateway.
- Six subnets across two Availability Zones:
  - Two private CloudFront-origin/ALB subnets.
  - Two public application-task subnets.
  - Two private future-database subnets.
- A public route table attached only to the application subnets.
- An RDS subnet group using the two database subnets.

It reserves the future PostgreSQL location but creates no database.

security.tf (infra/platform/security.tf)

Defines network firewall rules:

- Reads AWS’s existing CloudFront origin-facing IP prefix list.
- Creates an ALB security group.
- Allows port 80 into the ALB only from CloudFront’s origin-facing addresses.
- Allows the ALB to contact the task only on Streamlit port 8501.
- Creates the task security group.
- Allows task ingress only from the ALB.
- Allows task outbound access for OpenAI, Cognito key retrieval, and AWS services.

There is deliberately no inbound rule for FastAPI port 8000 because Streamlit reaches it inside the same ECS task.

registry.tf (infra/platform/registry.tf)

Defines image and secret storage:

- Creates the ECR container-image repository.
- Makes image tags immutable.
- Enables vulnerability scanning when images are pushed.
- Retains only the ten newest images through a lifecycle policy.
- Refuses recursive repository deletion.
- Creates the Secrets Manager container for the OpenAI API key.

Terraform creates only the secret container—not a secret value—so the credential never enters Terraform configuration or state.

identity.tf (infra/platform/identity.tf)

Defines operator identity resources:

- Creates the Cognito user pool.
- Disables public sign-up.
- Creates the operators group.
- Creates Cognito’s hosted-login domain.
- Creates the application’s OAuth client.
- Enables authorization-code flow only, not implicit tokens.
- Registers the CloudFront callback and sign-out URLs.
- Configures one-hour access/ID tokens and a one-day refresh token.

The built-in Cognito provider is temporarily enabled so the client can exist before Google is configured. The later federation unit will add Google and remove this transitional configuration.

runtime.tf (infra/platform/runtime.tf)

Defines the running application environment:

- Creates a CloudWatch log group with seven-day retention.
- Creates the ECS task-execution role:
  - Pulls images from ECR.
  - Sends logs to CloudWatch.
  - Reads the OpenAI secret.
- Creates the application task role, which currently has no AWS permissions.
- Creates the ECS cluster.
- Defines a Fargate task containing two containers:
  - FastAPI on port 8000.
  - Streamlit on port 8501.
- Pins both containers to the same exact image digest.
- Injects Cognito configuration and the OpenAI secret.
- Makes Streamlit wait until FastAPI is healthy.
- Creates the internal Application Load Balancer, target group, and listener.
- Creates the ECS service, stopped by default.
- Enables automatic rollback when a new ECS deployment fails its health checks.

The task gets a public IP for outbound access, but no public listener exposes it directly.

edge.tf (infra/platform/edge.tf)

Defines the public HTTPS edge:

- Registers the internal ALB as a CloudFront VPC origin.
- Creates a cache policy with all caching disabled.
- Creates an origin-request policy forwarding cookies, query parameters, headers, and WebSocket-related traffic.
- Creates the CloudFront distribution.
- Redirects HTTP users to HTTPS.
- Uses CloudFront’s default trusted *.cloudfront.net certificate.
- Restricts the distribution to the lowest-cost CloudFront price class.

CloudFront becomes the only public application entry point.

outputs.tf (infra/platform/outputs.tf)

Reports operational values needed after an apply:

- Public CloudFront URL.
- Application callback URL.
- Google OAuth callback URL.
- Cognito issuer, user-pool ID, and client ID.
- ECR repository URL.
- ECS cluster and service names.
- OpenAI secret ARN.
- Future PostgreSQL subnet-group name.

These outputs connect Terraform to the later Google setup, image delivery, smoke-test, rollback, and teardown procedures.

## Supporting configuration files

These are not ordinary .tf definitions, but they are part of the workflow:

- *.tfvars.example: safe templates for Terraform input variables.
- *.tfbackend.example: safe templates describing where remote state lives.
- .terraform.lock.hcl: pins exact provider packages and checksums.
- platform.tftest.hcl (infra/platform/tests/platform.tftest.hcl): mocked tests that verify important safety and architecture properties without calling AWS.

The key mental model is: each directory describes a desired state, Terraform compares that desired state with its saved state and the real AWS account, then proposes the minimum operations needed to reconcile them. terraform plan shows those proposed operations; only terraform apply performs them.
